extracted.intended_audience: IP practitioners, in-house counsel, inventors and companies seeking to protect and enforce IP rights in Singapore
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guide to obtaining, exploiting and enforcing intellectual property rights in Singapore, with emphasis on patentability standards, filing/prosecution options, term/renewal, assignment formalities and enforcement mechanisms. Useful for applicants, attorneys and rights-holders planning Singapore filings or litigation strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark registrability (distinctiveness requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs which function as badges of trade origin and distinguish one trader’s goods or services from another can be registered as trademarks. Typical candidates are words, devices and logos. Non-traditional signs such as shapes, colours, sound and motion marks can and have been registered in Singapore, provided the signs are graphically represented and are capable of distinguishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon registration the proprietor obtains the exclusive right to use the mark for specified goods/services under the Nice Classification. Protection can extend to similar signs on similar goods/services and, for well-known marks, even to dissimilar goods/services. Term is 10 years from filing and renewable in 10-year blocks; revocation for non-use applies if not genuinely used for five years. Registration procedure: file nationally with IPOS or via Madrid Protocol; IPOS conducts formality check and examines absolute (distinctiveness, descriptiveness) and relative grounds (conflicts with earlier marks); published for 2-month opposition period. Fast-track (Trade Marks Fast) available for national applications (first office action/acceptance in 3–6 weeks in simple cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark assignment and licence formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments and licences of registered trademarks are ineffective unless in writing and signed by or on behalf the grantor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grantee should record transactions with the IPOS Registry — failing to record means they will not bind third parties without notice and may prevent recovery of damages or an account of profits for any infringement until the assignment/transaction is registered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent can be granted in Singapore for an invention that is new, inventive and capable of industrial application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain subject matter is excluded (discoveries, scientific theories, mathematical methods, aesthetic creations, methods for performing a mental act, playing a game or doing business and presentation of information). Treatment and surgical methods are not considered industrially applicable. There is a limited 12-month grace period for disclosures in narrow circumstances (disclosure by inventor or person who obtained matter directly/indirectly from inventor, breach of confidence, display at an international exhibition or before a learned society).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term and annuities
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard term of a Singapore patent is 20 years, subject to the payment of annuities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent term can be extended by up to five years if certain conditions are met, including unreasonable delay by the patent office in granting the patent, or a delay in opportunity to exploit the patent due to the need to obtain marketing approval for a pharmaceutical product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership of employee inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention made by an employee in the course of employment is generally taken to belong to the employer, and no specific assignment is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the default rule for employee-created inventions unless contractually varied; parties should nonetheless consider contractual clarity for ownership and remuneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent filing routes and priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applications can be filed in Singapore via the domestic national route, or through the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In accordance with the Paris Convention, Singapore allows applicants to claim up to 12 months’ priority based on the date of first filing in another Paris Convention member country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent examination timing and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: IPOS conducts examination of each patent application to ensure it meets patentability requirements. Examination is requested 36 months from the priority date but can be extended with a fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It typically takes two to three years for the final examination report depending on objections raised. A unique feature: IPOS may rely on a corresponding international search report, or search reports from specified offices (Australia, Canada [filed in English], EPO [filed in English], Japan, South Korea, New Zealand, U.S. or UK).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH) and acceleration options
rubrics_metrics.description: IPOS is part of the Global Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH) programme and has bilateral PPH programmes. PPH requests are generally considered favourably and accelerate examination by reducing duplicity of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To encourage PPH use IPOS is offering a 30% discount on the examination fee until December 31, 2027, if PPH is requested. There is also an option to pay a fee to accelerate examination and receive an office action within four or eight months if PPH is not available. Regional acceleration programmes include ASEAN Patent Examination Cooperation (ASPEC) and collaborative search and examination with neighbouring offices (Cambodia, Laos, Indonesia, Vietnam).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent assignment and licence formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments and licenses must be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the grantor; grantees should record transactions with the IPOS Registry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to record transactions will not bind third parties without notice and may prevent the grantee from recovering damages or an account of profits for infringement until registered. (Note: this reiterates the formal requirements and practical consequences.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Licence of right and compulsory licences
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may make the patent available as a licence of right to allow others to use the invention and will reduce the renewal fees by half. A compulsory licence may also be granted to a third party to remedy an anti-competitive practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licence of right is a voluntary mechanism to encourage use; compulsory licences are statutory measures intended to address competition/public interest concerns and encourage exploitation of inventions in Singapore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent linkage system for therapeutics
rubrics_metrics.description: Singapore has a patent linkage system where a party applying to register a therapeutic product needs to declare to the Health Sciences Authority whether there is a restraining patent for the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a restraining patent is in force and the applicant is not the patentee, the applicant must notify the patentee who can commence infringement proceedings to invoke a 30-month moratorium on the therapeutic product application. This links regulatory approval timelines with patent enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright subsistence conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative outputs attract copyright protection if the Copyright Act’s requirements of territorial connection, fixation and originality are met. There is no registration regime for copyright in Singapore; protection is automatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusive rights attach to expressive elements and do not encompass mere information (raw factual data). Proprietors seeking to protect sensitive information may consider law of confidence, PDPA or contractual confidentiality instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright ownership default rules and assignment formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: By default, the first owner of copyright in a work is its maker; employee-created works are an exception — copyright in works created in the course of employment vests in the employer without need for assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments and exclusive licences are ineffective unless signed in writing by the grantor. Copyright that will come into existence in the future can be assigned/licensed by its prospective owner. There is no recordal mechanism for copyright assignments/licences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational Data Analysis (CDA) exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The CDA exception permits reproduction of works for the sole purpose of identifying, extracting and analysing information or data from the works via a computer program, once a person has lawfully obtained access to copyrighted works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exception does not permit circumvention of technological protection measures (e.g. paywalls) and, unlike some foreign counterparts, is not constrained to non-commercial use — it can be used by commercial actors. Implemented in 2021 as part of SIPS 2030 to facilitate AI training and analytics workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright terms by type of work
rubrics_metrics.description: Different categories of copyrightable works have bespoke terms of protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial works (literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works): author’s lifespan + 70 years. Sound recordings: 70 years from first publication. Films: 70 years from first publication. Broadcasts and cable programmes: 50 years from the end of the year of broadcast/programme’s first inclusion in a cable service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial design registrability and exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs of articles (features responsible for physical appearance) can be registered; these include shape, configuration, colours, pattern or ornament, but not methods/principles of construction or features dictated by functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration available only if the design is new — i.e., not registered or published anywhere in the world before the filing date. A 12-month grace period applies for certain disclosures (e.g., by the designer or through abuse of confidence). Registered designs that lack novelty are vulnerable to revocation. Singapore expanded regime in 2017 to include non-physical products with utilitarian functions (virtual keyboards, whiteboards, musical instruments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design rights scope and term
rubrics_metrics.description: A registered design confers the proprietor the exclusive right to prevent others from using the design in Singapore, including making, importing, selling, hiring or offering for sale or hire any article to which the design or a substantially similar design has been applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial term of protection is five years from filing; protection can be renewed in 5-year blocks up to a maximum of 15 years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design registration procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: National design applications filed via IPOS must include representations identifying the relevant article or non-physical product and its Locarno Classification; Hague System international applications designating Singapore are filed with WIPO and forwarded to IPOS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPOS conducts formalities examination; if acceptable, registration typically issues in about four months. Paris Convention priority allowed (6 months). IPOS is exploring regional accelerator programmes (e.g., Cambodia-Singapore cooperation) to complement standard examination timeframes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary remedies for IP infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal remedies for infringement include injunctions, damages, an account of profits and orders for delivery up or destruction of infringing goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other notable remedies: statutory damages for use of counterfeit trademarks; statutory and additional damages for copyright infringement; dynamic injunctions under the Copyright Act permitting site-blocking orders that may be varied over time to counter circumvention by infringers. Civil remedies are complemented by border enforcement and criminal measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Border enforcement and criminal liability for serious infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil remedies are complemented by strong border enforcement and criminal measures in Singapore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serious infringements (e.g., selling goods with falsely applied trademarks) may be investigated by the Intellectual Property Rights Branch of the Singapore Police Force and result in criminal liability. Rights holders can work with Singapore Customs to prevent import/export of infringing goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: IP litigation venues and case management
rubrics_metrics.description: IP disputes are adjudicated in the High Court by specialist judges assigned to the IP/IT list; a simplified process is available for smaller-scale or straightforward matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For complex cross-border commercial disputes, the Singapore International Commercial Court (SICC) handles cases, supported by specialist international judges; appeals from SICC can go to the Singapore Court of Appeal. The specialist judiciary and active case management aim to provide efficient resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative dispute resolution options for IP
rubrics_metrics.description: Singapore complements its courts with a comprehensive range of ADR mechanisms for IP disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IP disputes are arbitrable. Major institutions: Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC) — awards enforceable in >170 jurisdictions under the New York Convention; Singapore International Mediation Centre (SIMC) for confidential mediation with experienced IP mediators; WIPO Centre (only office outside Geneva located in Singapore) for IP-focused arbitration/mediation. These provide complementary local and international platforms for confidential and efficient dispute resolution.
